prompt: What is Dataflow, in Beam's terms?
hint: Beam has a word for what executes a pipeline.

choices.text: A runner: Google's managed service for Beam pipelines
choices.why: Right. The program is Beam; Dataflow is one of the places it runs.

choices.text: A language of Google's for writing streaming jobs instead of Beam
choices.why: The pipeline is written in Beam, in Python, Java or Go. Dataflow reads none of your source.

choices.text: A library that replaces Beam's own transforms on Google Cloud
choices.why: The same Beam program is sent to Dataflow unchanged; only `--runner` differs.

choices.text: The Pub/Sub feature that delivers messages in order
choices.why: That is ordering keys, lesson 19. Dataflow is compute, not messaging.

prompt: What makes a PCollection unbounded?
hint: Compare a file with a subscription.

choices.text: It has no last element
choices.why: Right: more messages may always arrive. A subscription never says it is finished; a file does.

choices.text: It holds more elements than fit in memory
choices.why: A bounded file of a terabyte is still bounded. The difference is whether it ends, not its size.

choices.text: It was read with `ReadFromText`
choices.why: `ReadFromText` reads a file, which ends: that is a bounded PCollection.

choices.text: Its elements have no timestamps
choices.why: Elements from a stream carry timestamps, the publish time by default.

prompt: Python reaches the line `lines | 'Parse' >> beam.FlatMap(parse)`. What happens at that moment?
hint: Beam builds first and runs after.

choices.text: Every line is parsed, and the result is kept in memory
choices.why: Nothing is read yet. Parsing happens when the runner executes the graph.

choices.text: A step is added to the graph, and nothing is parsed yet
choices.why: Right. The runner decides later how, and where, `parse` runs.

choices.text: The function `parse` is sent to Dataflow
choices.why: Nothing is sent anywhere until the pipeline is run, and here the runner is local.

choices.text: Beam checks that `parse` handles every bad line
choices.why: Beam cannot know what a function does with its input. A mistake in it shows up when the pipeline runs.

prompt: A colleague runs `orders_beam.py` with `--runner=DirectRunner` on a laptop with internet access and gets different log lines from the lesson. Why?
hint: In Beam 2.76.0 the DirectRunner is a switch.

choices.text: The emulator answers differently when the laptop is online
choices.why: The emulator is local in both cases. The difference is in which runner Beam chose.

choices.text: Beam 2.76.0 refuses `--runner=DirectRunner` and picks Dataflow
choices.why: Dataflow is only ever chosen by name, and it needs a project and the `gcp` extra.

choices.text: With GitHub reachable, Beam ran it on Prism instead
choices.why: Right. Offline it fell back to the runner inside Python; that is why the lesson names `BundleBasedDirectRunner`.

choices.text: The DirectRunner writes logs only when it has no network
choices.why: It logs in both cases. What it logs differs because it ran on a different runner.

prompt: Which step of `PlacedTotals` needs elements to change workers on Dataflow?
hint: Only one step brings elements together.

choices.text: `Parse`, which turns a line into an event
choices.why: It looks at one line at a time, so any worker can do any line.

choices.text: `Placed`, which keeps the placed events
choices.why: A filter decides for each element alone.

choices.text: `Add`, the `CombinePerKey`
choices.why: Right. Every placed order of one neighbourhood has to meet, and that is the shuffle.

choices.text: `Format`, which writes the window
choices.why: It formats one total at a time, after the combine.

prompt: The export ends with a line cut in the middle. What does `orders_beam.py` do with it?
hint: Look at what `parse` yields when `json.loads` fails.

choices.text: It stops the whole pipeline at that line, with a `JSONDecodeError`
choices.why: That is what a `parse` without the `try` would do, and then there would be no totals at all.

choices.text: It skips the line in silence
choices.why: Silence would leave the totals one order short with nothing saying so.

choices.text: It sends the line to a second output, written to its own file
choices.why: Right: `unreadable-00000-of-00001.txt` holds it, whole.

choices.text: It counts the line as an order of zero reais
choices.why: The line never becomes an event; it never reaches `Placed`.

prompt: Why may `add` not be written as "count the pairs and sum the second fields of the original events"?
hint: Beam calls a combining function on parts, and then on the parts' results.

choices.text: Because some pairs are earlier results, already holding counts above one
choices.why: Right. Counting pairs would count a partial sum of fifty orders as one order.

choices.text: Because Beam passes it a dictionary, not pairs
choices.why: `Key` made the values `(1, cents)` pairs, and partial results keep that shape.

choices.text: Because Python cannot sum tuples
choices.why: `add` sums them field by field, and that works.

choices.text: Because the original events are lost after `Parse`
choices.why: They are not lost, but `add` only ever sees the values of one key.

prompt: The night run wrote five totals, of 150, 138, 161, 140 and 152 orders. How many of the 2,000 events were `placed`?
hint: Each placed event is one order in one total.

prompt: Run with `--streaming --window 0`, what does the pipeline do?
hint: The global window of an unbounded collection never ends.

choices.text: It runs and publishes the totals once a minute
choices.why: There is no window to close once a minute: `--window 0` removed it.

choices.text: It runs and never publishes anything
choices.why: Beam does not let it get that far.

choices.text: It refuses to start, before any message
choices.why: Right: a group in the global window with the default trigger. The `ValueError` arrives before any message is read.

choices.text: It falls back to batch and reads the subscription once
choices.why: Beam has no such fallback; an unbounded source stays unbounded.

prompt: The stream run published its totals with the window `15:33:00`, on the afternoon of 30 October. The events say 15 October, from 19:00. Why?
hint: Ask where `ReadFromPubSub` takes an element's timestamp from.

choices.text: The emulator rewrites the field `at` on the way through
choices.why: Nothing touched the message bodies; the same bytes arrived.

choices.text: `Format` converts every time to the current day
choices.why: `Format` only formats the window it is given.

choices.text: Its time is when Pub/Sub received it, without a timestamp attribute
choices.why: Right. The window is in publish time; lesson 22 reads the time from the event instead.

choices.text: Fixed windows always start at the moment the pipeline itself starts
choices.why: Fixed windows are aligned to the clock, minute by minute, whenever the pipeline started.

prompt: On the DirectRunner, the pipeline dies after pulling 500 messages and before publishing their window. What happens to those 500 when it is started again?
hint: Look at when this runner acknowledges a message.

choices.text: They are counted twice, as at-least-once delivery predicts
choices.why: That would need them to be delivered again, and they were already acknowledged.

choices.text: They are lost: it acknowledged each one when it pulled it
choices.why: Right. Dataflow acknowledges only after the work is kept durably, which is the opposite trade.

choices.text: They are counted once, as Pub/Sub removes the duplicates
choices.why: There are no duplicates here, only messages nobody will deliver again.

choices.text: They wait in the dead-letter topic
choices.why: No dead-letter topic was configured, and nothing failed delivery.

prompt: Which of these changed between the night run and the stream run? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the two ends and the middle.

choices.text: Where the lines were read from
choices.why: A file in one, a subscription in the other.

choices.text: The window the totals belong to
choices.why: `all` in batch, one minute of publish time in stream.

choices.text: The steps of `PlacedTotals`
choices.why: The same five steps ran in both; that is the point of the composite.

choices.text: The totals per neighbourhood
choices.why: They came out the same to the cent, because one window held every message.

choices.text: Where the unreadable line went
choices.why: A file in batch, the topic `order-totals-unreadable` in stream.

prompt: A streaming job on Dataflow has to stop, and the totals already counted in the open minute must be published. Which command?
hint: One of the two ends at once.

choices.text: `gcloud dataflow jobs cancel`
choices.why: Cancel stops at once and loses the open windows.

choices.text: `gcloud dataflow jobs drain`
choices.why: Right. Drain stops reading, closes the open windows, emits them and ends.

choices.text: `gcloud dataflow jobs list --status=active`
choices.why: That lists the jobs; it stops nothing.

choices.text: Running the program again with `--update`
choices.why: Update replaces the code and keeps the job running.

prompt: Why does a streaming worker without Streaming Engine default to a 400 GB disk?
hint: Ask where the windows' state lives.

choices.text: It keeps its share of the windows' state on its own persistent disk
choices.why: Right. With Streaming Engine the service keeps it, and 30 GB is enough.

choices.text: It stores every message it has read, for replay
choices.why: Replay is Pub/Sub's job, from the subscription; the worker keeps state, not a copy of the stream.

choices.text: Pub/Sub requires a disk of that size on each subscriber
choices.why: Pub/Sub sets no requirement on a subscriber's disk.

choices.text: A bigger disk makes the worker's processor faster
choices.why: A Persistent Disk's size sets its throughput, not the processor's speed; the reason is the state.

prompt: Quitanda wants the nightly totals launched by Cloud Composer with a different `--input` each night, and one night's input needs an extra step in the graph. Which kind of template fits?
hint: One kind fixes the graph's shape when it is staged.

choices.text: A classic template, because its parameters are runtime values
choices.why: A classic template fixes the graph when it is staged; a runtime value cannot add a step.

choices.text: No template: Composer runs the program from the analyst's laptop
choices.why: Composer has no laptop to run from, and a schedule should not depend on one.

choices.text: A Flex Template, which builds the graph at each launch
choices.why: Right. The container runs the program at launch, so parameters can change the graph.

choices.text: A Google-provided template
choices.why: Those are fixed pipelines for common copies; this one is Quitanda's own.

prompt: Match each Dataflow feature to what it does.
hint: Two of them are about the shuffle, in different modes.

pairs.right: Moves a batch job's shuffle off the workers into the service
Keeps a stream's shuffle and window state in the service
Resizes a worker's memory and bills in DCUs
Starts a batch job within six hours, for a lower price

right_distractors: Lets a classic template add steps at launch

prompt: A batch job shuffles 1,024 GiB. With the page's volume adjustment, how many GiB are billed?
hint: A quarter of the first 250, half of the rest up to 5 TiB.

prompt: One streaming worker of 2 vCPU runs the whole month, 730 hours, at 0.1035 dollars a vCPU-hour in São Paulo. What do its vCPUs alone cost, in dollars?
hint: vCPUs times hours times the price.

prompt: The streaming job costs about 183 dollars a month and the nightly batch about 4. When is the stream worth it?
hint: Both give the same totals; the difference is when.

choices.text: When the data grows larger than what one worker's memory holds
choices.why: Batch handles any size by adding workers; size does not decide between the two.

choices.text: When the totals feed something that acts within the minute
choices.why: Right. A report read in the morning gets the same answer from the night run.

choices.text: Whenever the events already arrive through Pub/Sub
choices.why: They also land in the nightly export, which the batch reads for a fraction of the price.

choices.text: When FlexRS is not available in the region
choices.why: FlexRS only discounts batch; its absence would make batch dearer, not the stream worth it.

prompt: Put in order what happens to one placed order in the stream run.
hint: The window comes before the middle.
items: `ReadFromPubSub` pulls the message and acknowledges it
The message is placed in the minute it was published in
`Parse` and `Placed` keep it as a placed order
`Add` adds it to its neighbourhood's total for that minute
The total is published to `order-totals` when the minute closes

prompt: To send `orders_beam.py` to Google instead of running it here, the option to change is `--___`.
hint: The program sets a default for it.

prompt: Which part of `orders_beam.py` would have to change to read the nightly export from Cloud Storage on Dataflow?
hint: Only the ends know where data lives.

choices.text: `PlacedTotals`, so that it reads from a bucket
choices.why: The composite never knows where its lines come from.

choices.text: `add`, to combine across workers
choices.why: It already works in any grouping, which is what workers need.

choices.text: Nothing: the paths and runner are options
choices.why: Right. `--input gs://…`, `--output gs://…` and `--runner=DataflowRunner`, with the `gcp` extra installed.

choices.text: `Format`, to write a window other than `all`
choices.why: A batch over a file is still in the global window on Dataflow.
